extracted.intended_audience: USPTO practitioners (patent agents/attorneys), trademark correspondents, and USPTO disciplinary counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used by the USPTO Administrative Law Judge to evaluate alleged misconduct by a registered practitioner (patent agent/attorney) in trademark and patent matters, and to determine sanctions. Covers burdens of proof, signature/TEAS rules, what constitutes practice before the Office, powers of attorney requirements, defenses, and sanctioning factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO statutory authority to suspend or exclude (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the Office if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis for discipline; it encompasses incompetence, disreputability, gross misconduct, and regulatory violations. Used as the foundational threshold for initiating disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable professional rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.100 et seq. and prior Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.100 et seq.) apply to persons who practice before the Office and became effective May 3, 2013; for alleged violations occurring prior to that date, the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20 et seq.) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which regulatory regime governs alleged conduct by reference to the effective date; apply the appropriate set of rules when evaluating alleged violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Thereafter, Respondent bears the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision quotes authorities defining clear and convincing as an intermediate standard 'between a preponderance of the evidence and proof beyond a reasonable doubt' and requiring evidence 'of such weight that it produces... a firm belief or conviction.' Use this heightened standard when assessing the sufficiency of proof for both allegations and affirmative defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sign trademark documents (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark documents that require verification must be sworn to in a declaration signed by the owner or the owner's authorized representative. Properly authorized signatories include (i) a person with legal authority to bind the owner (e.g., corporate officer), (ii) a person with firsthand knowledge of the facts and actual or implied authority to act on behalf of the owner, or (iii) an attorney with power of attorney from the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For juristic entities (corporations), additional requirements apply: a corporate officer must sign when legal authority to bind the corporation is required. Improper signatories render verifications deficient and may be misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firsthand knowledge requirement for verified declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations verifying facts in trademark documents must be made by someone with firsthand knowledge of the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A signatory cannot rely solely on another person's firsthand knowledge; the declarant must actually have firsthand knowledge. Entering an applicant's signature when the filer lacks firsthand knowledge fails this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable TEAS signature methods (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three acceptable signature methods for TEAS filings: (1) direct signature — the signatory personally enters his/her own electronic signature between two forward slashes (permitted characters: letters, numbers, spaces, punctuation); (2) ESign-on — text version e-mailed to signatory who returns signed electronic copy; (3) HSign-on — scanned pen-and-ink handwritten signature attached as .pdf/.jpeg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TEAS deletes signatures when saving a .pdf copy, requiring the user to re-sign before submission. An acceptable electronic signature must be personally entered by the named signatory (or use an authorized ESign/HSign procedure). The Court interprets the regulation to mean no other electronic signature forms are acceptable unless the Director authorizes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of attorney and authorization requirements (TMEP § 611.06 and 37 C.F.R. § 2.17(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A power of attorney's nature and extent of authority must be ascertained from the instrument itself; for corporations, a power of attorney must be signed by a corporate officer. Merely stating that a person has been granted authority is insufficient; documents must expressly state authority to legally bind the applicant under its bylaws or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers labeled 'Power of Attorney' that are merely cut-and-pasted declarations listing contact information do not prove legal authority to bind an applicant. Even signed powers may be insufficient if they do not convey the specific authority required (and non-attorneys generally cannot perform legal services by virtue of a POA where practice of law is restricted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limits of practice before the Office in trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.14 and § 11.5(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.14 identifies who may practice in trademark matters: (a) attorneys; (b) non-lawyers recognized before January 1, 1957; and (c) specially recognized foreign attorneys. Practice includes consulting or giving advice in contemplation of filing, preparing and prosecuting applications, preparing amendments requiring written argument, conducting oppositions/cancellations/appeals, etc. An individual not authorized may act as a domestic representative or correspondent only in limited ways (serving as contact/address for foreign applicants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparing, electronically signing, and filing applications, responses to Office Actions, and Statements of Use goes beyond mere domestic representative duties and constitutes unauthorized practice before the Office when done by persons not authorized under §11.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic representative role vs. unauthorized practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A domestic representative is appointed to provide a contact and address for service of process for foreign applicants; forwarding correspondence and serving as an address is permissible, but preparing, verifying, signing, and prosecuting trademark matters constitutes practice before the Office and requires authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a correspondent's address or email while actually performing prosecution tasks (entering signatures, submitting responses, creating documents) is impermissible if the correspondent is not authorized to practice. Concealment of continued active conduct after exclusion is an aggravating circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature identification requirement (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: For all trademark correspondence that requires a signature, the signature must be either a handwritten signature of the signatory, or an electronic signature that is personally entered by the person named as the signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner is the proper signatory, they must identify themselves and personally enter their own signature (e.g., their own name between slashes), rather than entering another person's signature. Entering someone else's signature without identifying that the filer is the person signing is misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct examples constituting grounds for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of misconduct include: entering the electronic signatures of applicants and filing those documents; filing trademark documents prepared by foreign attorneys not authorized to practice before the Office; actively practicing in trademark matters while only authorized as a domestic representative; and continuing to act as domestic representative after an exclusion order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct may constitute deceitful conduct, aiding unauthorized practice of law, making false/misleading representations to the Office, and other violations of USPTO disciplinary rules; these examples inform the application of statutory and regulatory disciplinary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court consults ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions to identify aggravating factors (dishonest motive, pattern of misconduct, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing) and mitigating factors (e.g., lack of prior disciplinary record). These factors guide whether to impose maximum sanctions (e.g., exclusion) or lesser sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include dishonest motive, pattern and extent of misconduct, and refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing; a mitigating factor noted is lack of prior disciplinary record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of aggravating factors supports more severe sanctions (potential maximum sanction/exclusion). Lack of prior discipline may mitigate. The decision applies these when recommending exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED investigation and procedural duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director is authorized to investigate possible grounds for discipline, must notify the practitioner in writing of the initiation of an investigation, and may request information and evidence from the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no regulatory requirement that OED request specific documents; a practitioner's refusal to produce documents or pleading the Fifth may limit what the OED could have known, but does not itself invalidate the investigation. Procedural objections must be evaluated against the regulatory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional standard for discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: All practitioners engaged in practice before the Office are subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Office. The violation of any USPTO disciplinary rule constitutes a ground for discipline under § 11.19(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration as a patent agent/attorney subjects one to USPTO discipline for conduct before the Office even if alleged acts relate to trademark matters rather than patent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for affirmative defenses (selective enforcement and Contract Clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective enforcement: to prevail, Respondent must show (1) she was singled out while similarly situated persons were left untouched, and (2) the prosecution was pursued invidiously or in bad faith (based on impermissible considerations). Contract Clause: to claim impairment, a party must show existence of contract, law impaired the contract, and impairment was substantial; Contract Clause claims typically apply to state legislation and not federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defenses require specific proof; mere allegation of others' similar conduct is insufficient without showing investigation/enforcement disparity and invidious motive. Contract Clause defenses are unlikely to succeed against federal regulatory action absent special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential sanction/remedy: exclusion and post-order responsibilities (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60, 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may order exclusion from practice in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters. Practitioners are directed to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 regarding responsibilities during suspension/exclusion, and § 11.60 concerning petitions for reinstatement; 37 C.F.R. § 11.55 describes appeal rights to the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion is an available sanction where factors warrant it. The decision documents the Court's consideration of sanctioning factors and provides notice of appeal and reinstatement procedures.
